c: effective: a free promise to keep an offer open is not binding
ineffective: he promised to keep the offer open until Friday
ineffective: the promise created an option in the buyer's favor
effective only if the buyer agrees in writing to release him
ex: An offer may be revoked at any time before acceptance is communicated, even if the offeror promised to keep it open, unless that promise was paid for. A paid promise is an option.

1: An unpaid promise to hold an offer open can be withdrawn.
2: An option needs consideration. Nothing was paid here.
3: The buyer's agreement is not needed to revoke an offer.

q: A buyer offers $350,000 with closing on June 30. The seller signs the offer but changes the closing date to July 15 and returns it. What exists now?
c: A binding contract with closing on June 30
ex: An acceptance must mirror the offer. Any change, however small, is a counteroffer: it terminates the buyer's offer and makes the seller the new offeror. There is no contract unless the buyer accepts.

0: A changed term means there was no acceptance.
2: The buyer's original offer was terminated by the counteroffer.
3: No contract exists yet, so nothing is voidable.

q: A buyer delivers a written offer to a seller. Before the seller accepts, the buyer dies. The offer:
c: binds the buyer's estate if the seller then accepts
ex: An offer ends on the death or insanity of either party before acceptance.

0: Death before acceptance ends the offer. The estate is not bound.
2: No 30-day rule keeps the offer open.
3: An option is a separate, paid-for contract.

q: An offer becomes a contract when:
c: the offeree signs it, whether or not the offeror is told
the acceptance is communicated to the offeror
the deposit is placed in escrow
ex: A contract is formed when the offeree accepts and the acceptance is communicated to the offeror. Until then the offeror may still revoke.

0: A private decision is not an acceptance.
3: A deposit is not what forms the contract.

q: An investor pays an owner $2,000 for a 60-day option to buy a lot for $300,000. On day 45 the investor decides not to buy. The investor:
c: is in breach of the option contract
must buy the lot or pay damages
may recover the $2,000 from the owner
ex: The optionee holds a choice, not a duty. If she does not exercise the option she loses only the option money. The optionor (the owner) is the party who is bound.

0: The optionee has no duty to buy.
3: The option money paid for the owner's promise and is not returned.

q: Before it is exercised, an option to buy real estate is a:
c: bilateral contract that binds both parties
unilateral contract that binds only the optionor
unilateral contract that binds only the optionee
void agreement until the option money is repaid
ex: An option is unilateral: only the owner (optionor) has made a binding promise. When the optionee exercises it, it becomes a bilateral sale contract.

0: It becomes bilateral only when the option is exercised.
2: The optionee holds the choice. The optionor is bound.
3: A paid option is a valid contract.

q: A sale contract says that if the buyer defaults, the seller keeps the $10,000 deposit as agreed damages. This amount is:
ex: Liquidated damages are an amount agreed in advance, so the actual loss need not be proved. The deposit is the usual example.

0: Compensatory damages are measured by the actual loss proved.
2: Specific performance is a court order to perform the contract.
3: Rescission undoes the contract and returns the parties to their original positions.

q: Which remedy cancels the contract and puts both parties back where they were before it was signed?
ex: Rescission unwinds the contract and restores both parties to their original positions.

0: Specific performance forces the contract to be carried out.
1: Liquidated damages are a pre-agreed sum of money.
3: Compensatory damages pay for the loss. They do not undo the contract.

q: Courts may order specific performance of a real estate sale contract mainly because:
c: every parcel of land is unique
real estate contracts must be in writing
the buyer has paid a deposit
ex: Land is unique, so money may not replace the property the buyer chose. That is why a court can order the breaching party to perform.

1: The writing requirement is the statute of frauds. It is not the reason for this remedy.
2: A deposit is not the reason.

q: A sale contract says nothing about assignment. The buyer transfers her rights under it to her brother. The assignment is generally:
c: valid, because contracts are assignable unless they prohibit it
void, because sale contracts are never assignable
valid only with the FREC's approval
void, because the brother did not sign the original contract
ex: Contracts are generally assignable unless the contract prohibits it. Personal-service contracts, such as listings, are the exception.

1: Sale contracts are assignable unless they say otherwise.
2: The FREC does not approve assignments.
3: An assignee does not need to have signed the original contract.

q: In a Florida sale, legal title passes to the buyer when:
c: the contract is signed by both parties
the deed is delivered and accepted
ex: Signing the contract gives the buyer equitable title. Legal title passes at closing by delivery and acceptance of the deed. Recording comes afterwards and gives notice to others.

0: Signing the contract gives equitable title only.
3: Recording gives notice. Title has already passed by delivery and acceptance.

q: A buyer offers $400,000. The seller counters at $415,000. Before the buyer answers, the seller receives a better offer and withdraws her counteroffer. The withdrawal is:
c: effective: a counteroffer may be revoked before it is accepted
ineffective: a counteroffer must stay open for 24 hours
ineffective: the buyer's original offer still binds the seller
effective only if the buyer has not yet paid a deposit
ex: A counteroffer is a new offer, and the seller is now the offeror. Like any offer, it may be revoked before acceptance is communicated.

1: No rule keeps a counteroffer open for 24 hours.
2: The buyer's offer was terminated by the counteroffer.
3: A deposit does not affect the right to revoke.

q: A seller signs an exclusive right of sale listing. During the listing period she sells the house to her neighbor without any help from the broker. The broker is owed:
c: nothing, because the seller found the buyer
ex: Under an exclusive right of sale listing the brokerage is paid no matter who sells the property, including the owner.

0: That is the result under an exclusive agency or open listing.
3: The full commission is owed, not expenses.

q: An owner gives open listings to Brokers A, B and C. Broker B shows the house to the buyer and negotiates the sale. Who earns a commission?
c: All three brokers share it equally
Broker A, who took the first listing
No one, because open listings pay no commission
ex: Under an open listing only the broker who is the procuring cause of the sale is paid. The other brokers receive nothing.

2: Being first to list earns nothing.

q: Under which listings may the owner sell the property herself without owing a commission?
c: Exclusive right of sale and exclusive agency
ex: The owner keeps the right to sell personally, free of commission, under an open listing and under an exclusive agency listing. Under an exclusive right of sale the commission is owed no matter who sells.

0: Exclusive agency also leaves the owner free to sell.
1: An open listing also leaves the owner free to sell.
3: Under exclusive right of sale the owner owes the commission even on her own sale.

q: By statute, a written listing agreement must include each of the following EXCEPT:
c: the balance of the seller's mortgage
ex: A written listing must contain a definite expiration date, a description of the property, the price and terms, the fee or commission, and the principal's signature. The mortgage balance is not on the list.

0: A definite expiration date is required. The question asks for the exception.
1: A property description is required. The question asks for the exception.
2: The fee or commission is required. The question asks for the exception.

q: A written listing agreement says it lasts 'until the property is sold'. The agreement:
c: is proper, because both parties freely agreed to the term
violates license law: it has no definite expiration date
is proper, as long as the seller initials that clause
is void under the statute of limitations
ex: A written listing agreement must have a definite expiration date. A licensee who omits it can be disciplined by the FREC.

0: Agreement does not replace the required definite expiration date.
2: Initials do not cure the missing date.
3: The statute of limitations sets the time to sue.

q: During the listing period the seller dies. The listing agreement:
c: continues and binds the seller's heirs
ex: A listing terminates by performance, expiration, mutual agreement, abandonment, destruction of the property, or the death or incapacity of either party.

0: Death of a party ends this personal-service contract.
2: Listings do not convert to another type.
3: Death ends the listing before its expiration date.

q: A listing agreement is best described as:
c: a contract between the seller and the sales associate
an employment contract between the seller and the brokerage
a contract that transfers equitable title
ex: A listing is a personal-service (employment) contract in which the seller hires the brokerage to find a buyer. It belongs to the brokerage, not to the individual associate.

0: The contract is with the brokerage.
2: Equitable title comes from a signed sale contract.
3: An option gives a buyer the right to purchase.

q: A seller tells a broker: 'I need $280,000 from the sale. Anything above that is yours.' The house sells for $305,000. Under this net listing the broker receives:
ex: In a net listing the broker keeps whatever the sale brings above the seller's set net price: $305,000 − $280,000 = $25,000.

0: That is 5% of the price. A net listing is not a percentage commission.
1: That is 6% of the price. A net listing pays the excess over the seller's net.
3: That is 10% of the price. A net listing pays the excess over the seller's net.

q: Which listing gives the broker the most protection?
ex: Under an exclusive right of sale the brokerage is paid no matter who sells, even the owner. It is the strongest and the standard form.

0: Under an open listing only the procuring broker is paid.
1: A net listing describes how the fee is measured, not who is protected.
2: Under exclusive agency the owner may sell without paying.

q: A sales associate obtains a signed written listing at 3 p.m. on Tuesday. By when must the seller receive a copy?
ex: A copy of a written listing agreement must be given to the person signing within 24 hours of obtaining it.

2: Three business days is the broker's escrow deposit deadline.
3: The copy is due within 24 hours.

q: The associate who took a listing leaves Brokerage A and joins Brokerage B. The seller is happy with her work. The listing:
c: moves with the associate to Brokerage B
ex: The listing is the brokerage's contract with the seller. It stays with Brokerage A when the associate leaves, and it cannot be assigned to another brokerage without the seller's consent.

0: The listing belongs to the brokerage, not the associate.
2: An associate's departure does not end the listing.
3: Listings are not shared this way.

q: Unless the parties agree in writing on a different period, the buyer of a house built in 1970 must be given how long to conduct a lead-based paint inspection or risk assessment?
ex: Buyers of housing built before 1978 get a 10-day opportunity for a lead-based paint inspection or risk assessment, unless the parties agree in writing on a different period or the buyer waives it in writing.

0: Three days is the HOA disclosure cancellation period.
1: Seven days is the condominium resale cancellation period.
3: Fifteen days is the cancellation period for a condominium bought from the developer.

q: A tenant is about to lease an apartment built in 1965. Under the lead-based paint rule the tenant is entitled to:
c: the disclosure and pamphlet, plus a 10-day inspection period
the disclosure and pamphlet, but no inspection period
nothing, because the rule covers sales only
a lead-free certificate from the landlord
ex: The rule covers sales and leases of housing built before 1978. Tenants receive the disclosure and the pamphlet, but the 10-day inspection opportunity is for buyers only.

0: The 10-day period is for buyers, not tenants.
3: The rule requires disclosure, not a lead-free certificate.

q: A buyer in a homeowners' association community receives the HOA disclosure summary only after signing the contract. The buyer may void the contract:
c: within 3 days after receiving it or before closing, whichever is first
within 15 days after receiving it or before closing, whichever is first
within 7 days after receiving it, not counting weekends and holidays
at any time before or after closing, because the right cannot be waived
ex: The HOA disclosure summary is due before the contract is signed. If it is late, the buyer may void the contract within 3 days after receiving it or before closing, whichever comes first. The right cannot be waived, and it ends at closing.

1: Fifteen days is the period for a condominium bought from the developer.
2: Seven days is the condominium resale period.

q: Under current law, the buyer of a resale condominium unit may cancel within how long after signing the contract and receiving the required documents?
c: 3 days, not counting Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays
7 days, not counting Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays
10 days, not counting Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays
15 days, not counting Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays
ex: Since July 1, 2025 the resale cancellation period is 7 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays. Older books say 3 business days, which is outdated. A developer sale gives 15 days.

0: Three business days is the old rule, replaced on July 1, 2025.
2: Ten days is the lead-based paint inspection period.
3: Fifteen days applies to a purchase from the developer.

q: A buyer who signs a contract to buy a new condominium unit from the developer may cancel within:
ex: A buyer from the developer has 15 days to cancel. A resale buyer has 7 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays. Both rights end at closing.

0: Three days is the HOA disclosure period.
1: Seven days is the resale period.
2: Ten days is the lead-based paint inspection period.

q: The property tax disclosure summary given to a buyer of residential property warns the buyer:
c: that property taxes are paid a year in advance
not to rely on the seller's current property tax bill
that the homestead exemption transfers to the buyer
that taxes cannot rise more than 3% after the sale
ex: The summary warns the buyer not to rely on the seller's current taxes. A sale or improvements can trigger a reassessment, so the buyer's taxes may be much higher.

0: Property taxes are paid in arrears.
2: The seller's exemption does not transfer.
3: The 3% cap protects a continuing homestead owner. A sale resets the assessment.

q: Florida's energy-efficiency rating law requires that a buyer of a building receive:
c: an energy rating of the property paid for by the seller
information about the option of an energy-efficiency rating
an energy certificate before the listing is advertised
a 10-day period to obtain an energy audit
ex: The buyer receives information about the option of having an energy-efficiency rating done. No rating or certificate of the property is required.

0: No rating is required. That resembles the Portuguese energy certificate.
2: Florida requires information, not a certificate.
3: Ten days is the lead-based paint inspection period.

q: A sale contract states that 'time is of the essence'. This means:
c: the closing must take place within 30 days
the contract deadlines are strictly enforceable
the contract expires if the deposit is a week late
the parties may extend deadlines orally
ex: 'Time is of the essence' makes every deadline strictly enforceable: missing one, even by a day, is a breach.

0: The clause sets no particular closing period.
2: The clause makes deadlines strict. It does not set a one-week rule.
3: The clause makes deadlines stricter, not looser.

q: A seller sells AS IS. Termite damage hidden inside a wall, unknown to the seller, is found by the buyer after closing. Under Johnson v. Davis the seller:
c: is liable, because AS IS never excuses any defect
is liable, because sellers guarantee the condition of the home
is not liable under this rule: the seller did not know of the defect
is not liable, because AS IS cancels every disclosure duty
ex: Johnson v. Davis requires a seller to disclose known facts that materially affect value and are not readily observable. A defect the seller does not know about is outside the rule.

0: The duty covers known defects only.
1: Sellers do not guarantee the home's condition.
3: AS IS does not cancel the duty to disclose known latent defects.

q: Three years ago a homicide took place in a house now for sale. The buyer has not asked about the home's history. Must the seller or the licensee disclose it?
c: Yes, because any death on the property is a material fact
Yes, but only when the sale is financed by a federally related loan
No, because by statute it is not a material fact to be disclosed
No, but only when the property is sold under an AS IS contract
ex: By statute, the fact that a homicide, suicide or death occurred on the property, or that an occupant had HIV or AIDS, is not a material fact that must be disclosed.

0: The statute says a death on the property is not a material fact that must be disclosed.
1: Financing does not change the rule.
3: The rule applies to every sale, not only AS IS sales.

q: Under the FR/BAR 'AS IS' contract, the buyer:
c: gives up the right to inspect the property
may inspect and cancel within the inspection period
may require the seller to make all repairs
must close even if serious defects are found
ex: AS IS means the seller makes no repairs. The buyer keeps a due-diligence right to inspect and to cancel within the inspection period.

0: The buyer keeps the right to inspect.
2: AS IS means the seller is not obliged to repair.
3: The buyer may cancel within the inspection period.

q: A house is not in a mapped flood zone and has never flooded. The seller of this residential property must:
c: give no flood disclosure, because the home is outside a flood zone
give the buyer the flood disclosure at or before contract execution
give the flood disclosure only if the buyer asks for it in writing
give the flood disclosure at closing, together with the deed
ex: A seller of residential real property must give the buyer the flood disclosure at or before the time the sales contract is executed. The duty is not limited to mapped flood zones.

0: The disclosure is required for residential sales, inside or outside a flood zone.
2: The buyer does not have to ask.
3: It is due at or before contract execution, not at closing.

q: A contract has a financing contingency. The buyer applies for the loan in good faith and is denied. The buyer may generally:
c: cancel and receive the deposit back
be forced to close with cash
sue the lender for specific performance
ex: A contingency is a condition that must be met for the contract to go forward. If the financing contingency fails in good faith, the buyer may cancel and the deposit is returned.

1: The deposit is returned when a contingency fails in good faith.
2: The contingency protects the buyer from having to close without the loan.
3: Specific performance is a remedy between the contract parties, not against a lender.

q: The federal lead-based paint disclosure rule does NOT apply to:
c: the sale of a house built in 1960
a one-year lease of an apartment built in 1975
the sale of a house built in 1985
the sale of a duplex built in 1950
ex: The rule covers sales and leases of housing built before 1978. A house built in 1985 is outside it.

0: A 1960 house is covered. The question asks which is NOT covered.
1: Leases of pre-1978 housing are covered. The question asks which is NOT covered.
3: A 1950 duplex is covered. The question asks which is NOT covered.

q: A landlord rents out a house built in 2022. Is Florida's radon notice required?
c: No, the notice is for sales only
No, the notice is for buildings built before 1978
Yes, for the sale or rental of any building
Yes, but only if radon has been detected
ex: The radon notice is required for the sale or rental of any building, on at least one document signed at or before the contract or rental agreement.

3: The notice is required whether or not radon has been found.

q: The document in which the borrower personally promises to repay the debt is the:
ex: The promissory note is the debt: the borrower's personal written promise to repay. The mortgage is the security instrument that pledges the property.

0: The mortgage pledges the property. The promise to pay is in the note.
3: A satisfaction is recorded after the loan is paid off.

q: In a mortgage loan, the mortgagee is the:
ex: The borrower gives the mortgage, so the borrower is the mortgagor. The lender receives it and is the mortgagee. '-or gives, -ee receives.'

2: The seller is not a party to the mortgage unless the seller is financing the sale.
3: The title company is not a party to the mortgage.

q: Which document pledges the property as security for the debt?
ex: The mortgage is the security instrument: it pledges the property as collateral for the note.

0: The note is the personal promise to pay.
2: The sale contract is between buyer and seller.
3: The closing statement lists the money, it pledges nothing.

q: Which clause lets the lender demand the full balance if the owner transfers the property without the lender's consent?
ex: A due-on-sale (alienation) clause makes the balance due when the property is transferred. It blocks an assumption without the lender's consent.

0: Acceleration is triggered by default, not by a transfer.
2: Defeasance ends the lien when the loan is paid in full.
3: Subordination changes the priority of liens.

q: A developer has one mortgage covering 40 lots. Which clause lets him free each lot from the mortgage as it is sold?
ex: A release clause frees individual parcels from a blanket mortgage, which is one mortgage covering several parcels.

1: An exculpatory clause removes the borrower's personal liability.
2: A prepayment clause deals with paying the loan early.
3: A receivership clause lets a receiver collect rents during foreclosure.

q: A land seller who took back a mortgage agrees that the buyer's later construction loan will have first priority. This is done with a:
ex: In a subordination clause a lien agrees to take a junior (lower-priority) position, here behind the construction lender.

0: A release clause frees parcels from a blanket mortgage.
1: Defeasance ends the lien on full payment.
3: Due-on-sale makes the balance due on a transfer.

q: A mortgage says the borrower has no personal liability and the lender may look only to the property. This is:
ex: With an exculpatory clause the lender's only recourse is the property. If a foreclosure sale falls short, there is no deficiency claim against the borrower.

0: Acceleration makes the whole balance due on default.
1: Defeasance ends the lien on full payment.

q: Which clause provides that the lender's lien ends when the loan is paid in full?
ex: The defeasance clause is the promise that the lien is defeated on full payment. The recorded satisfaction is the proof.

1: Acceleration makes the whole balance due on default.
2: A release clause frees single parcels from a blanket mortgage.

q: After a mortgage loan is paid in full, who must have the satisfaction of mortgage recorded?
c: The closing agent who handled the purchase
ex: Within 60 days after receiving full payment, the mortgagee (or the holder or servicer) must sign a satisfaction, have it acknowledged, record it, and send the recorded satisfaction to the borrower.

0: The duty is on the lender, not the borrower.
2: The duty is on the lender.
3: The property appraiser values property for taxes.

q: Acceleration and due-on-sale clauses both make the whole balance due. What triggers each one?
c: Acceleration: a transfer. Due-on-sale: a default
Acceleration: a default. Due-on-sale: a transfer
Both are triggered only by a default
Both are triggered only by full payment
ex: Acceleration is triggered by the borrower's default. Due-on-sale is triggered by a transfer of the property.

2: Due-on-sale is triggered by a transfer.
3: Full payment ends the loan. It triggers neither clause.

q: A buyer finances a home in Florida with a bank loan. After closing, who holds legal title to the home?
c: The bank, until the loan is paid
A trustee, under a deed of trust
The bank and the buyer jointly
ex: Florida is a lien-theory state. The borrower holds legal title and the lender holds a lien on the property as security.

1: Deeds of trust are used in title-theory states.
3: The lender holds a lien, not title.

q: Which clause deals with the borrower's right to pay the loan off early, or a penalty for doing so?
ex: A prepayment clause gives a right to pay early or sets a penalty for doing so.

1: Defeasance ends the lien when the loan is fully paid.
3: Acceleration is the lender's right on default.

q: A buyer assumes the seller's mortgage. The lender does not agree to a novation. The buyer later defaults and the foreclosure sale leaves a deficiency. Who may be liable?
c: The buyer only, as the new owner
The seller only, as the original borrower
Both the buyer and the seller
Neither, because the loan was assumed
ex: A buyer who assumes a loan becomes personally liable. Without a novation the seller stays secondarily liable, so the lender can look to both.

0: Without a novation the seller is still liable.
1: That is the result when the buyer takes 'subject to' the mortgage.
3: Both made, or kept, a promise to pay.

q: Mortgage foreclosure in Florida is:
c: nonjudicial, under a power of sale
judicial: a court action ending in a public sale
carried out by a trustee under a deed of trust
an administrative process run by the DBPR
ex: Florida foreclosure is judicial. The lender must file a court action, which ends in a public sale.

0: Florida lenders cannot foreclose without a court.
2: Trustee sales belong to title-theory states.
3: The DBPR has no role in foreclosure.

q: After a Florida foreclosure sale, how long does the former owner have to redeem the property?
c: 10 days from the date of the sale
30 days from the date of the sale
1 year from the date of the sale
No time: the right ends at the sale
ex: The equity of redemption lasts until the foreclosure sale. Florida has no statutory right of redemption after the sale.

0: Florida gives no redemption period after the sale.
1: Florida gives no redemption period after the sale.
2: Some states allow this. Florida does not.

q: A foreclosure sale brings $30,000 more than the first mortgage debt and costs. There is also a $20,000 second mortgage on the property. Who receives the surplus?
c: The second lender receives $20,000 and the borrower $10,000
The second lender and the borrower each receive $15,000
ex: A surplus goes to the junior lienors first, then to the borrower. The second mortgagee is paid its $20,000 and the remaining $10,000 goes to the borrower.

0: Junior lienors are paid before the borrower.
1: The first lender is entitled only to its debt and costs.
3: The surplus is not split equally.

q: A lender agrees to let a homeowner sell for less than the loan balance and to accept the sale proceeds. This is a:
ex: In a short sale the property is sold and the lender agrees to accept less than the amount owed.

0: In a deed in lieu the borrower deeds the property to the lender.
2: A novation substitutes a new borrower and releases the old one.
3: A foreclosure is a court action, not an agreed sale.

q: A borrower in default offers the first lender a deed in lieu of foreclosure. The property also has a second mortgage. Why might the first lender prefer to foreclose?
c: A deed in lieu always takes longer than a court foreclosure
With a deed in lieu the lender takes title subject to the second mortgage
A deed in lieu must first be approved by the FREC
A deed in lieu gives the borrower one year to redeem the home
ex: A deed in lieu is faster, but the lender takes title subject to junior liens. A foreclosure can eliminate them.

0: A deed in lieu is faster.
3: No redemption period follows a deed in lieu.

q: On the closing statement, a mortgage assumed by the buyer is entered as a:
c: credit to the seller and a debit to the buyer
debit to the seller and a credit to the buyer
debit to both the seller and the buyer
ex: The buyer takes over the seller's debt, so the seller is charged (debit) and the buyer is given credit toward the price.

2: The buyer is credited, not debited.
3: There is also a debit to the seller.

q: A buyer assumes an existing $150,000 mortgage. The intangible tax was paid when the loan was made and the debt is unchanged. Which taxes are due on the assumed loan?
c: Documentary stamps on the note only
Both note stamps and intangible tax
ex: Note stamps ($0.35 per $100) are due on new and assumed mortgages. The intangible tax (2 mills) applies to new mortgages only.

1: The intangible tax is for new mortgages only.
2: The intangible tax is not charged again on an assumption.
3: Note stamps are due on an assumed mortgage.

q: A lender has accelerated the loan and filed for foreclosure. To redeem before the sale, the borrower must pay:
c: the entire balance of the debt
half of the balance, with a payment plan
the missed payments plus one extra payment
ex: The equity of redemption lets the borrower stop the foreclosure by paying in full. After acceleration, 'in full' means the whole debt.

0: After acceleration the whole balance is due.

q: A buyer who takes title 'subject to' the seller's existing mortgage:
c: becomes personally liable for the debt
has no personal liability for the debt
releases the seller from the debt
must obtain a novation from the lender
ex: A 'subject to' buyer makes the payments but promises the lender nothing. If the loan goes into default, only the original borrower faces a deficiency.

2: Only a novation releases the seller.
3: A novation belongs to an assumption with a release.

q: A foreclosure sale brings less than the amount owed. The court judgment for the unpaid balance is a:
ex: A deficiency judgment is a judgment for the unpaid balance against the parties who are personally liable on the note.

1: A satisfaction records that a loan was paid in full.
2: A lis pendens is a notice of a pending lawsuit.
3: A novation substitutes a new borrower.

q: Gross monthly income is $6,000. Principal and interest are $1,300 a month, property taxes $2,400 a year and insurance $1,200 a year. What is the housing expense ratio?

0: That divides by annual income ($72,000). Use monthly income.
1: That uses principal and interest only. PITI includes taxes and insurance.

q: Using the 28% / 36% benchmarks, a borrower has gross monthly income of $7,000 and other monthly debts of $700. What is the maximum PITI?
ex: Housing limit: 28% × 7,000 = $1,960. Total limit: 36% × 7,000 = $2,520, minus $700 of debts = $1,820. The maximum PITI is the lower of the two: $1,820.

0: The debts are subtracted from the 36% limit, not from the 28% limit.
2: $1,960 passes the housing ratio but fails the total ratio.
3: $2,520 is the total limit before subtracting the other debts.

q: Which income figure do the qualifying ratios use?
ex: Both ratios divide by gross monthly income, the income before taxes and deductions.

0: Take-home pay is the Portuguese habit. Florida exam ratios use gross income.
2: The ratios use gross monthly income.
3: The ratios use gross monthly income.

q: In the housing expense ratio, PITI stands for principal, interest:
ex: PITI is principal, interest, property taxes and homeowner's insurance.

0: T and I are property taxes and homeowner's insurance.
2: T and I are property taxes and homeowner's insurance.
3: T and I are property taxes and homeowner's insurance.

q: Under the course's benchmarks, a conventional borrower's housing and total obligations ratios should not exceed:
ex: Conventional: 28% housing and 36% total. FHA: 31% and 43%. These are course conventions, not statutes.

3: The order is reversed. Housing is the smaller number.

q: On a loan of $600,000, interest is not usurious under Florida law unless it exceeds:
ex: The 18% simple-interest ceiling applies to loans of $500,000 or less. For loans over $500,000 the ceiling is in effect 25%.

0: 10% is not a Florida usury ceiling.
1: 18% applies to loans of $500,000 or less.
3: 45% is where criminal usury becomes a felony.

q: Willfully and knowingly charging interest of 50% a year on a loan, where no other law allows it, is:
c: lawful if the borrower agrees in writing
ex: Criminal usury: more than 25% and up to 45% a year is a second-degree misdemeanor. More than 45% is a third-degree felony.

0: The borrower's agreement does not legalize usury.
1: The misdemeanor tier is above 25% up to 45%.

q: A lender persuades a homeowner to refinance four times in three years, collecting new fees each time, with no real benefit to the borrower. This practice is:
ex: Loan flipping is repeated refinancing to collect fees.

0: Equity stripping is lending that drains the owner's equity.
2: Packing is adding hidden add-on products.
3: Balloon abuse is the misuse of a lump final payment.

q: Adding hidden, unneeded products such as extra insurance to a loan is the predatory practice called:
ex: Packing means loading a loan with hidden add-on products.

1: Loan flipping is repeated refinancing for fees.
2: Equity stripping drains the owner's equity.
3: Steering is a fair housing violation.

q: A private lender makes a $300,000 loan at 22% a year simple interest. No other law allows that rate. The loan is:
c: lawful, because the rate is under 25%
ex: The loan is $500,000 or less, so the ceiling is 18% and 22% is usurious. Criminal usury begins only above 25%.

0: The 25% ceiling is for loans over $500,000.

q: Gross monthly income is $7,500, PITI is $2,025 and other monthly debts are $675. Under the 28% / 36% benchmarks, does the borrower qualify?
c: No, the housing ratio is above its benchmark
No, the total ratio is above its benchmark
Yes, both ratios are within the benchmarks
Only if the other debts are ignored
ex: Housing: 2,025 ÷ 7,500 = 27%. Total: (2,025 + 675) ÷ 7,500 = 36%. A ratio exactly at the benchmark passes, because the limit is 'should not exceed'.

1: The total ratio is exactly 36%, which passes.
3: Both ratios pass with the debts included.

q: The SAFE Act requires which people to be licensed and registered through the NMLS?
ex: The SAFE Act requires mortgage loan originators to be licensed and registered through the Nationwide Multistate Licensing System (NMLS).

0: Sales associates are licensed under Chapter 475.
3: The SAFE Act covers mortgage loan originators.

q: The owner's right to sell, give away or leave the property by will is the right of:
ex: Disposition is the right to transfer the property. The bundle of rights is possession, control, enjoyment, exclusion and disposition.

0: Possession is the right to occupy.
1: Exclusion is the right to keep others out.
2: Enjoyment is the right to use the property without interference.

q: An owner deeds land to a church 'so long as it is used for church purposes'. The church holds a:
ex: A fee simple defeasible can be lost if a stated condition occurs or is broken. A fee simple absolute has no conditions.

0: A fee simple absolute has no conditions.
2: A life estate is measured by a life.
3: A leasehold is possession under a lease, not ownership.

q: Ana deeds her house 'to Bruno for life' and says nothing more. At Bruno's death the house returns to Ana or her heirs. Ana's interest is a:
ex: When the property comes back to the grantor or the grantor's heirs, the future interest is a reversion. A remainder goes forward to a third person.

0: A remainder goes to a third person named in the deed.

q: A deed gives property 'to Bruno for the life of Carla'. Bruno's estate is a:
ex: A life estate measured by another person's life is a life estate pur autre vie. It ends when Carla dies.

1: A defeasible fee depends on a condition, not a life.
2: A tenancy at will is a leasehold.
3: A remainder is the future interest that follows a life estate.

q: A life tenant leases the house to a tenant for five years. Two years later the life tenant dies. The lease:
c: continues for the three years that remain
ends, because the life tenant could not lease more than she had
becomes a month-to-month tenancy with the remainderman
binds the remainderman if it was recorded
ex: A life tenant may sell or lease her interest, but a sale or lease by the life tenant ends at the measuring death.

0: The lease ends with the life estate.
2: The lease does not convert. It ends.
3: Recording does not extend the life tenant's interest.

q: During a life estate, who pays the property taxes and the upkeep?
c: The remainderman and the life tenant equally
ex: The life tenant enjoys the property, so she pays the taxes and upkeep and must not commit waste.

1: The grantor has given the life estate away.
3: The life tenant alone carries these costs.

q: Which of the following is a freehold estate?
ex: Freehold estates are ownership estates of indefinite duration: fee simple absolute, fee simple defeasible and the life estate. The others are leaseholds.

0: An estate for years is a leasehold with a fixed term.
1: A tenancy at will is a leasehold.
3: A tenancy at sufferance is a holdover leasehold.

q: A tenant's lease expires. She stays in the apartment without the landlord's consent. Her tenancy is now:
ex: A holdover tenant who stays without the landlord's consent has a tenancy at sufferance.

1: A periodic tenancy renews with the landlord's agreement.
2: A tenancy at will exists with the landlord's consent.

q: Under current Florida law, how much written notice is needed to end a month-to-month residential tenancy?
ex: Current s. 83.57: year to year 60 days, quarter to quarter 30, month to month 30, week to week 7. The old 15-day rule for month to month is outdated.

0: Seven days is for a week-to-week tenancy.
1: Fifteen days is the old rule. It is now 30.
3: Sixty days is for a year-to-year tenancy.

q: How much written notice is needed to end a year-to-year residential tenancy in Florida?
ex: Year to year 60 days, quarter to quarter 30, month to month 30, week to week 7.

0: Fifteen days is an outdated month-to-month figure.
1: Thirty days is for quarter-to-quarter and month-to-month tenancies.

q: How much written notice is needed to end a week-to-week residential tenancy in Florida?
ex: Week to week needs 7 days' written notice before the end of a period.

2: Fifteen days is an outdated month-to-month figure.
3: Thirty days is for month-to-month and quarter-to-quarter tenancies.

q: A written lease runs from June 1 to August 31. What must the landlord do for it to end on August 31?
ex: A lease with a fixed term is an estate for years. It ends automatically on its end date, without notice.

1: Notice periods apply to periodic tenancies.
2: Notice periods apply to periodic tenancies.
3: Notice periods apply to periodic tenancies.

q: A tenant pays a fixed rent and the landlord pays the property taxes, insurance and maintenance. This is a:
ex: In a gross lease the tenant pays fixed rent and the landlord pays the property's expenses.

1: In a net lease the tenant pays some or all of the expenses.
2: A percentage lease adds a share of sales.
3: A ground lease is a lease of land on which the tenant builds.

q: A lease states that rent will rise by a set amount on each anniversary. This is a:
ex: A graduated (step-up) lease raises the rent on a schedule written in the lease. An index lease ties the rent to an index such as the CPI.

1: An index lease follows an outside index such as the CPI.
2: A percentage lease depends on the tenant's sales.
3: A gross lease describes who pays the expenses.

q: A tenant with 14 months left on her lease lets a friend take the apartment for 6 months. The friend pays the tenant, who keeps paying the landlord. This is:
ex: A sublease transfers part of the remaining term or space. The subtenant pays the tenant, who stays primarily liable to the landlord.

0: An assignment transfers the entire remaining term.
2: A novation substitutes a new party and releases the old one.
3: A tenancy at sufferance is a holdover without consent.

q: A tenant assigns her lease. The landlord does not release her. The assignee stops paying rent. The original tenant is:
c: primarily liable, as in a sublease
liable only for damage to the unit
ex: After an assignment the assignee pays the landlord, but the original tenant stays secondarily liable unless the landlord releases her.

2: Primary liability is the rule in a sublease.

q: A two-year residential lease in Florida:
c: must be in writing and signed before two witnesses
must be in writing, with no witnesses required
may be oral if the rent is paid monthly
must be notarized and recorded to be valid
ex: A lease for more than one year must be in writing. Leases need no subscribing witnesses. Deeds still need two.

0: The two-witness rule for leases is outdated.
2: Only a lease of one year or less may be oral.
3: Notarizing and recording are not required for validity.

q: An apartment building is sold while its tenants' leases are still running. The leases:
c: end automatically on the day of closing
continue: the buyer takes title subject to them
end 30 days after the day of closing
continue only if the buyer agrees in writing
ex: A lease survives the sale of the property. The buyer takes title subject to the existing leases.

0: A sale does not end the leases.
3: The buyer's agreement is not needed.

q: A deed names 'John Smith and Mary Smith, husband and wife' as grantees and says nothing else. In Florida they hold title as:
ex: A deed to a married couple is presumed to create a tenancy by the entireties. Florida is not a community-property state.

0: That is the default for unmarried co-owners.
1: Joint tenancy needs express survivorship words.
3: Florida is not a community-property state.

q: To create a joint tenancy with right of survivorship in Florida, the deed must:
c: name the owners in alphabetical order
expressly state the right of survivorship
be signed by all the grantees
ex: Florida requires the four unities (possession, interest, time, title) plus express survivorship language. Without it, unmarried co-owners are tenants in common.

0: The order of names has no effect.
2: Grantees do not sign the deed.

q: Ana, Bruno and Carla own a lot as joint tenants with right of survivorship. Carla dies, leaving a will that gives everything to her son. Carla's interest passes to:
c: her son and Ana and Bruno in equal shares
ex: At a joint tenant's death her share passes to the surviving joint tenants, outside probate. A will cannot change that.

2: Escheat applies only when there is no will and no heirs.
3: The son receives nothing from this property.

q: A husband and wife own their home as tenants by the entireties. The husband dies, leaving a will that gives all his property to his brother. Who owns the home?
c: The wife and the brother as tenants in common
ex: Tenancy by the entireties has automatic survivorship. The surviving spouse owns the whole property, whatever the will says.

1: Survivorship gives the whole to the wife.
2: The will cannot pass entireties property.
3: The home passes outside the estate.

q: Which form of co-ownership is available only to a married couple?
ex: Only a married couple can hold as tenants by the entireties.

0: Anyone may be tenants in common.
1: Joint tenancy is not limited to spouses.
3: A tenancy at will is a leasehold.

q: One of three tenants in common wants to end the co-ownership. The other two refuse to buy her share or to sell. She may:
c: do nothing until the others agree
record a quitclaim deed for the whole property
ask the FREC to order a sale
ex: Any co-tenant may sue for partition, asking the court to divide the property or order its sale.

0: She does not need the others' agreement.
2: She can convey only her own share.
3: The FREC has no power over co-owners' property.

q: Which statement about tenants in common is correct?
c: A deceased owner's share passes to the surviving owners
Each may sell or will her own share without the others' consent
Only married couples may hold title this way
ex: Tenants in common may hold unequal shares. Each may sell, mortgage or will her own share, and there is no survivorship.

1: Survivorship belongs to joint tenancy and entireties.
3: That describes tenancy by the entireties.

q: A couple owns a house as tenants by the entireties. The husband signs a deed selling it to a buyer. The wife refuses to sign. The deed:
c: conveys the whole property to the buyer
conveys the husband's half to the buyer
conveys nothing: neither spouse can convey alone
is valid if it is recorded before she objects
ex: In a tenancy by the entireties neither spouse holds a separate half, and neither can convey alone.

0: One spouse cannot convey entireties property.
1: There is no separate half to convey.
3: Recording does not cure the missing signature.

q: Outside a municipality, Florida's constitutional homestead protection covers contiguous land of up to:
ex: The homestead protected from forced sale is up to 160 contiguous acres outside a municipality and 1/2 acre inside one.

0: 1/2 acre is the limit inside a municipality.

q: Which creditor can NOT force the sale of a Florida homestead?
c: The county, for unpaid property taxes
The lender that financed the purchase of the home
A roofer who was not paid for repairing the home's roof
A credit-card company holding a court judgment
ex: The homestead is exempt from forced sale by ordinary judgment creditors. Claims tied to the house get through: taxes and assessments, purchase money, and improvement, repair and labor on the property.

0: Property taxes can reach the homestead. The question asks who cannot.
1: The purchase mortgage can be foreclosed. The question asks who cannot.
2: Repair and labor claims on the property get through. The question asks who cannot.

q: Florida's homestead protection from forced sale is limited by:
c: value: the first $25,000 of the home's assessed value
value: the first $50,000 of the home's assessed value
land area: 1/2 acre in a municipality or 160 acres outside
price: the amount the owner originally paid for the home
ex: The creditor shield is measured in land, not dollars. The $25,000 figures belong to the homestead tax exemption, a different rule.

1: $50,000 is the total of the two tax exemptions.
3: The purchase price is not the test.

q: A married woman holds title to the couple's homestead in her name alone. To sell it:
c: she may sign the deed alone
her husband must join in the deed
she must first record a declaration of homestead
ex: The spouse must join in any deed or mortgage of the homestead, even when title is in one name.

0: Title in one name does not let her convey the homestead alone.
2: No court order is needed. The spouse's signature is.
3: No declaration is required to sell.

q: Besides the homestead, the Florida Constitution exempts how much personal property from forced sale?
ex: Article X, section 4 exempts $1,000 of personal property. It is not a land or tax figure.

2: $5,000 is a property tax exemption figure and an escrow limit.

q: The owner of a condominium unit holds:
c: shares in a corporation and a proprietary lease
fee simple title to the unit and an undivided share of the common elements
a leasehold in the unit for 99 years
fee simple title to the unit and to the land beneath it only
ex: A condominium unit is real property: the owner holds the unit in fee simple plus an inseparable undivided share of the common elements.

2: A condominium unit is owned, not leased.
3: The owner shares the common elements with the other owners.

q: A buyer's interest in a cooperative apartment is:
c: real property held in fee simple
ex: A cooperative buyer receives shares in the corporation that owns the building and a proprietary lease. That interest is personal property.

3: That is a form of co-ownership for married couples.

q: A timeshare buyer signs the contract on March 1 and receives the last required document on March 4. The right to cancel lasts until midnight of:
ex: A timeshare buyer may cancel until midnight of the 10th calendar day after the later of signing or receiving the last required document. March 4 + 10 days = March 14.

0: March 11 counts from signing. Count from the later date, March 4.
2: The days are calendar days, not business days.
3: Fifteen days is the developer condominium period.

q: A timeshare buyer wants to close in three days and offers to sign a waiver of the cancellation period. The waiver is:
c: valid, if it is in writing and signed
valid, if the developer agrees to it
not allowed: the right cannot be waived
valid, if a notary witnesses it
ex: The timeshare cancellation right cannot be waived, and closing before the period ends is unlawful.

0: A written waiver is still void.
1: The developer's agreement does not matter.
3: A notary cannot make the waiver valid.

q: Which buyer must receive the HOA disclosure summary?
c: The buyer of a condominium unit
The buyer of a cooperative apartment
The buyer of a timeshare interest
The buyer of a house in a mandatory HOA
ex: The HOA disclosure summary is for parcels in homeowners' association communities. It does not apply to condominiums, cooperatives or timeshares, which have their own rules.

0: Condominiums have their own disclosure and cancellation rules.
1: The HOA rule does not cover cooperatives.

q: A special-purpose unit of local government that finances a community's roads and utilities through assessments on the owners is a:
ex: A community development district (CDD) is a special-purpose local government that finances infrastructure through assessments. An HOA is an owners' association, not a government.

0: An HOA is a private owners' association.
2: A cooperative is a form of ownership.
3: A condominium association is a private owners' association.

q: A condominium buyer's statutory right to cancel the contract ends:
ex: The condominium cancellation rights (15 days from a developer, 7 days on a resale) end at closing. So does the HOA right.

1: The right does not survive closing.
2: The right does not survive closing.
3: The right ends at closing, not at recording.

q: The most probable price a property should bring in an arm's-length sale between informed parties under no unusual pressure is its:
ex: Market value is an estimate: the most probable price in an arm's-length sale between informed parties under no unusual pressure. Price is what was actually paid.

0: Price is a fact: what one buyer actually paid.
2: Assessed value is set for property taxes.
3: Insurable value is used for insurance.

q: The amount a buyer actually paid for a property is its:
ex: Price is what was paid. Cost is what it took to build. Market value is the most probable price.

0: Market value is an estimate, not what was actually paid.
1: Cost is what it took to build or produce.

q: Which value is used as the basis for property taxes?
ex: Assessed value is the value set for taxation. For a Florida homestead its yearly increase is capped, so it can be well below market value.

0: Market value is the most probable sale price.
3: Cost is what it took to build.

q: A parcel is useful, scarce and in demand, but its owner has no legal power to sell it. Which element of value is missing?
ex: Value needs all four elements at once: demand, utility, scarcity and transferability (DUST). Here the owner cannot transfer the property.

0: The question says the parcel is in demand.
1: The question says the parcel is useful.
2: The question says the parcel is scarce.

q: The first test of a property's highest and best use is whether the use is:
ex: The four tests, in order: legally permissible, physically possible, financially feasible, maximally productive.

0: Maximally productive is the last test.
1: Financially feasible is the third test.
2: Physically possible is the second test.

q: The income approach rests mainly on the principle of:
ex: Anticipation says value reflects expected future benefits. It is the basis of the income approach. Substitution is the foundation of the sales comparison approach.

1: Substitution supports the sales comparison approach.
2: Conformity is about similarity to the surroundings.
3: Regression is a superior home losing value among lesser ones.

q: An owner spends $85,000 on a pool. The pool raises the home's market value by $30,000. Under the principle of contribution, the pool is worth:
ex: Contribution: a feature is worth what it adds to value, not what it cost.

1: That is the cost minus the value added. Contribution is simply the value added.
2: $85,000 is the cost, not the contribution.
3: Cost and value added are not summed.

q: The largest and most expensive home in a neighborhood of modest homes tends to lose value. This is:
ex: Regression: a superior property loses value from lesser neighbors. Progression is the opposite.

0: Progression is a modest home gaining value from better neighbors.
2: Plottage is the extra value from combining parcels.
3: Anticipation is about expected future benefits.

q: A developer buys three adjoining lots and combines them. The combined site is worth more than the three lots separately. The extra value is called:
ex: Assemblage is the act of combining parcels. Plottage is the extra value that results.

0: Assemblage is the act of combining, not the value gained.
2: Progression is about a modest home among better ones.
3: Contribution is what one feature adds to value.

q: Value is best protected when a property is reasonably similar to its surroundings in size, style and use. This is the principle of:
ex: Conformity says value is best protected when a property is reasonably similar to its surroundings. Progression and regression follow from it.

0: Substitution: a buyer pays no more than the cost of an equal substitute.
1: Anticipation is about expected future benefits.
3: Contribution is what a feature adds to value.

q: Florida property is assessed for property tax purposes as of:
ex: Just value is determined as of January 1 each year.

3: November 1 is when the taxes become due and payable.

q: A comparable sold for $350,000. It has a garage worth $20,000 that the subject property lacks. What is the comparable's adjusted price?
ex: The comparable is better than the subject, so subtract: $350,000 − $20,000 = $330,000. Comp better, subtract.

0: The adjustment is made once, not twice.
3: A better comparable is adjusted down, not up.

q: A comparable sold for $280,000. The subject has a pool worth $18,000 and the comparable has none. What is the comparable's adjusted price?
ex: The comparable is inferior to the subject, so add: $280,000 + $18,000 = $298,000. Comp inferior, add.

0: An inferior comparable is adjusted up, not down.
3: The adjustment is made once, not twice.

q: A comparable sold for $425,000. It has an extra bedroom worth $15,000 that the subject lacks. The subject has a new roof worth $9,000 that the comparable lacks. What is the adjusted price?
ex: Subtract what the comparable has and the subject lacks; add what the subject has and the comparable lacks: $425,000 − $15,000 + $9,000 = $419,000.

0: Both adjustments were subtracted. The roof is added.
3: Both adjustments were added. The bedroom is subtracted.

q: In the sales comparison approach, adjustments are made to:
c: both the subject and the comparables
the listing prices of nearby homes
ex: Adjust the comparables, never the subject. Each comparable is changed to look like the subject.

3: The approach uses sales, not listings.

q: The sales comparison approach is most reliable for appraising:
ex: The sales comparison approach is best for homes and vacant land, where recent comparable sales exist.

0: Special-purpose buildings point to the cost approach.
1: Special-purpose buildings point to the cost approach.
3: Income property points to the income approach.

q: The amount of an adjustment for a feature should equal:
c: what the feature cost to install
what the feature adds to market value
the seller's estimate of its worth
ex: An adjustment is the feature's contribution to market value, not its cost.

0: Cost is not the measure. Contribution is.
2: Replacement cost belongs to the cost approach.
3: The market, not the seller, sets the adjustment.

q: After adjustment, comparable A ($300,000) needed one small adjustment, B ($310,000) needed five large ones, and C ($296,000) needed three. Which deserves the most weight?
c: A, with the fewest and smallest adjustments
B, with the highest adjusted price
C, with the lowest adjusted price
None: the three are simply averaged
ex: The comparable with the fewest and smallest adjustments is the most similar to the subject and gets the most weight. The appraiser weighs; she does not average.

1: The highest price does not earn more weight.
2: The lowest price does not earn more weight.
3: Reconciliation weighs. It is never a simple average.

q: Land value is $70,000. The building would cost $250,000 to build new and has $50,000 of accrued depreciation. What is the value by the cost approach?
ex: Value = land + cost new − accrued depreciation = $70,000 + $250,000 − $50,000 = $270,000.

0: The land value was left out.

q: Land value is $100,000. The building's cost new is $400,000 and it has depreciated 20%. What is the value by the cost approach?

0: That depreciates the land too. Land never depreciates.

q: A five-bedroom house has only one bathroom. This loss of value is:
ex: Functional obsolescence comes from outdated or poor design inside the property, such as one bathroom or no closets.

0: Physical deterioration is wear and tear.
2: External obsolescence comes from outside the property line.
3: Regression is a value principle about neighbors.

q: Worn-out carpet and peeling paint are examples of:
ex: Physical deterioration is wear and tear. It may be curable or incurable.

2: External obsolescence comes from outside the property.
3: Economic obsolescence is another name for external obsolescence.

q: Which type of depreciation is always incurable?
ex: External (economic) obsolescence is caused by something outside the property line, so the owner cannot cure it.

0: Physical deterioration may be curable or incurable.
1: Functional obsolescence may be curable or incurable.
3: Deferred maintenance is physical and usually curable.

q: The cost approach is most appropriate for appraising:
c: a 30-year-old house in a busy subdivision
an apartment building with a long rent history
ex: The cost approach is best for new construction and special-purpose properties such as schools, churches and fire stations.

0: An older home with many sales nearby calls for sales comparison.
2: Vacant land is valued by sales comparison.
3: Income property calls for the income approach.

q: The cost of building an exact replica of a structure, with the same materials and design, is its:
ex: Reproduction cost is the cost of an exact replica. Replacement cost is the cost of a building of equal utility using current materials and standards.

0: Replacement cost uses current materials and standards.
2: Market value is the most probable price.
3: Depreciated cost is cost new less depreciation.

q: Which statement about land in the cost approach is correct?
c: It is depreciated at the same rate as the building
It is valued by sales comparison and never depreciated
It is valued at its original purchase price
It is left out of the value estimate
ex: In the cost approach the land is valued separately by sales comparison and added to the depreciated cost of the improvements. Land never depreciates.

2: Land is valued at its current value by sales comparison.

q: An apartment building produces net operating income of $60,000 a year. Using a capitalization rate of 8%, what is its value?

0: That multiplies NOI by the rate. Divide.
1: That multiplies NOI by 8. Divide by 0.08.
3: The decimal point is misplaced: 8% is 0.08.

q: An investor pays $900,000 for a property with net operating income of $63,000. What is the capitalization rate?

3: That divides value by NOI. The rate is NOI ÷ value.

q: Potential gross income is $200,000. Vacancy and collection loss is 10%. Operating expenses are $70,000 and mortgage payments are $40,000. What is the net operating income?
ex: EGI = $200,000 − $20,000 = $180,000. NOI = $180,000 − $70,000 = $110,000. Mortgage payments (debt service) are not operating expenses.

0: Debt service is never deducted to find NOI.
2: The vacancy and collection loss was left out.
3: $180,000 is effective gross income, before operating expenses.

q: A duplex sold for $360,000. Its two units rent for a total of $3,000 a month. What is the gross rent multiplier?
ex: GRM = price ÷ monthly gross rent = $360,000 ÷ $3,000 = 120.

0: That uses annual rent ($36,000). GRM uses monthly rent.

q: The gross income multiplier (GIM) is based on:
ex: GIM = price ÷ annual gross income. GRM = price ÷ monthly gross rent.

0: Monthly rent is used for the GRM.
2: NOI is used with a capitalization rate.
3: Debt service is not part of either multiplier.

q: If the capitalization rate rises and net operating income stays the same, the property's value:
ex: Value = NOI ÷ rate. Dividing the same income by a higher rate gives a lower value.

0: A higher rate means a lower value.
2: Value changes whenever the rate changes.
3: A higher rate lowers the value.

q: A sales associate prepares a broker price opinion (BPO) for a lender. Which statement is correct?
c: She may charge for it, but may not call it an appraisal
She may call it an appraisal if her broker signs it
She may not charge any fee for a BPO
She needs an appraiser's license to prepare a BPO
ex: A licensee may prepare comparative market analyses and broker price opinions and may charge for them, but may never label them appraisals.

1: A BPO is never an appraisal, whoever signs it.
3: A real estate licensee may prepare BPOs and CMAs.

q: The standards that govern appraisal practice are known as:
ex: USPAP, the Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice, governs appraisal practice.

q: Effective gross income is:
c: potential gross income minus vacancy and collection loss
potential gross income minus operating expenses
net operating income minus debt service
ex: PGI − vacancy and collection loss = EGI. EGI − operating expenses = NOI.

1: Operating expenses are subtracted from EGI to reach NOI.
2: Debt service is outside the NOI calculation.
3: Depreciation is not part of this calculation.

q: Which item is an operating expense deducted to reach net operating income?
ex: Operating expenses are fixed expenses, variable expenses and reserves for replacements. Debt service and depreciation are not operating expenses.

0: Debt service is not an operating expense.
1: Depreciation is a tax deduction, not an operating expense.
3: The owner's income tax is not a property expense.

q: The income capitalization approach is most appropriate for appraising:
ex: The income approach is used for income-producing property.

0: A home is valued mainly by sales comparison.
1: A special-purpose building points to the cost approach.
3: Vacant land is valued by sales comparison.

q: Which of the following is NOT an authorized brokerage relationship in Florida?
ex: Florida authorizes three relationships: transaction broker, single agent and no brokerage relationship. Dual agency is prohibited.

0: Transaction broker is authorized. The question asks which is NOT.
1: Single agent is authorized. The question asks which is NOT.
3: No brokerage relationship is authorized. The question asks which is NOT.

q: In a single agent relationship, the party the licensee represents is called the:
ex: A single agent represents a principal. With a transaction broker or no brokerage relationship, the party is a customer.

0: A customer is not represented as a fiduciary.
2: The fiduciary is the agent, not the party represented.
3: A transaction broker is a type of licensee relationship.

q: Which brokerage relationship is a fiduciary relationship?
ex: Only the single agent is a fiduciary. A transaction broker gives limited representation and is not a fiduciary.

0: A transaction broker is not a fiduciary.
1: With no brokerage relationship there is no representation.
3: Only the single agent is a fiduciary.

q: Two sales associates work for the same brokerage. One is a single agent for the seller of a house. The other wants to be a single agent for the buyer of that house. This would be:
c: lawful, because two different associates are involved
lawful, if both parties consent in writing
prohibited dual agency by the brokerage
ex: The relationship belongs to the brokerage, so two associates each acting as single agent for opposite sides of a home sale is dual agency. Designated sales associates are allowed only in nonresidential deals.

0: The relationship is the brokerage's, not each associate's.
1: Consent allows a transition to transaction broker, never dual agency.
3: Designated sales associates are not allowed in a residential sale.

q: A licensee has been helping a buyer look at houses. Nothing was put in writing about their relationship. The licensee owes the buyer the duties of:
c: no one, because nothing was signed
ex: Unless a single agent or no brokerage relationship is established in writing, the licensee is presumed to be a transaction broker.

0: Single agency must be established in writing.
2: No brokerage relationship must be established in writing.
3: Without writing, the transaction-broker presumption applies.

q: A transaction broker provides:
c: full fiduciary representation of one party
limited representation to a buyer, a seller or both
ex: A transaction broker gives limited representation to the buyer, the seller or both. It is not a fiduciary.

3: That would be dual agency, which is prohibited.

q: A brokerage wants to work with both the buyer and the seller in the same home sale. The lawful way is to act as:
c: a dual agent, with written consent
a single agent for each party
a transaction broker for both parties
a single agent for the seller only, and ignore the buyer
ex: The lawful way to work both sides is to act as a transaction broker for both. If the brokerage started as single agent for one, that principal must first consent in writing to the transition.

0: Dual agency is prohibited even with consent.
1: Single agent for both sides is dual agency.
3: The buyer is still owed duties.

q: Which duty is owed even when there is no brokerage relationship?
ex: With no brokerage relationship the licensee owes three duties: honesty and fair dealing, disclosure of known material facts not readily observable, and accounting for all funds.

0: Loyalty belongs only to the single agent.
1: Obedience belongs only to the single agent.
3: Limited confidentiality is a transaction-broker duty.

q: How many duties does a transaction broker owe a customer?
ex: No brokerage relationship: 3 duties. Transaction broker: 7. Single agent: 9.

0: Three duties apply when there is no brokerage relationship.
3: Nine duties are the single agent's.

q: How many duties does a single agent owe a principal?
ex: No brokerage relationship: 3 duties. Transaction broker: 7. Single agent: 9.

0: Three duties apply when there is no brokerage relationship.
2: Seven duties are the transaction broker's.

q: Which of the following is a duty of a transaction broker?
ex: The transaction broker's seven duties include using skill, care and diligence. Loyalty, obedience, full confidentiality and full disclosure belong only to the single agent.

2: Full disclosure is a single-agent duty.

q: Which group of duties belongs only to the single agent?
c: Honesty, accounting and disclosure of material facts
Loyalty, obedience, full confidentiality and full disclosure
Skill, care, diligence and presenting all offers
Limited confidentiality and additional agreed duties
ex: Loyalty, obedience, full confidentiality and full disclosure are owed only by a single agent.

0: Those three are owed in every relationship.
2: Those are shared by transaction brokers and single agents.

q: The duty to present all offers and counteroffers in a timely manner is owed by:
c: both a transaction broker and a single agent
a licensee with no brokerage relationship
ex: Presenting all offers and counteroffers in a timely manner is on both the transaction broker's list of 7 and the single agent's list of 9. It is not one of the 3 duties owed with no brokerage relationship.

0: The transaction broker owes it too.
1: The single agent owes it too.
3: It is not one of the three duties owed with no brokerage relationship.

q: A transaction broker's limited confidentiality does NOT allow the licensee to keep secret:
c: that the seller will accept less than the asking price
that the buyer will pay more than the offered price
a known roof leak that is not readily observable
ex: Limited confidentiality protects price positions, motivations and information a party asks to keep confidential. It never overrides the duty to disclose known material facts that are not readily observable.

0: This is protected. The question asks what may NOT be kept secret.
1: This is protected. The question asks what may NOT be kept secret.
2: Motivation is protected. The question asks what may NOT be kept secret.

q: The duty to disclose known facts that materially affect the value of residential property and are not readily observable is owed:
c: by transaction brokers and single agents only
only when the buyer asks in writing
ex: Disclosure of known material facts is on all three duty lists: 3, 7 and 9.

0: It is owed in every relationship.
1: It is also owed when there is no brokerage relationship.
3: The buyer does not need to ask.

q: A single agent's duty of obedience requires the agent to follow the principal's:
c: instructions only when a commission is at stake
ex: Obedience covers lawful instructions only. An instruction to hide a known defect or to discriminate must be refused.

0: Unlawful instructions must not be followed.
2: Lawful oral instructions are covered too.
3: The duty does not depend on the commission.

q: A buyer tells his transaction broker that he would pay $15,000 more if he had to. The seller asks the same broker whether the buyer would go higher. The broker should:
c: tell the seller, because honesty requires it
tell the seller, because the broker also works with the seller
tell the seller only if the seller asks in writing
ex: Limited confidentiality forbids disclosing that a buyer will pay more than the offered price. Keeping that confidence is not dishonest.

0: Honesty does not require revealing protected price information.
1: The same limited confidentiality is owed to both customers.
3: Only the buyer can waive the confidentiality, in writing.

q: When must the No Brokerage Relationship Notice be given?
c: When the sale contract is signed
Within 3 business days after the first meeting
ex: The No Brokerage Relationship Notice is due before showing property. Each notice is tied to an event, not to a number of days.

1: That is too late. The notice comes before a showing.
2: At closing is always too late.
3: The notice is tied to the showing, not to a number of days.

q: A broker will act as single agent for a buyer. They plan to sign the representation agreement on Friday, but the broker shows the buyer a house on Wednesday. When is the Single Agent Notice due?
c: On Friday, when the agreement is signed
ex: The Single Agent Notice is due before or at the time of entering into a listing or representation agreement, or before showing property, whichever occurs first. Here the showing comes first.

1: The showing comes first, so the notice is due before it.
2: 24 hours is the deadline for a copy of a written listing.
3: At closing is always too late.

q: Which sale is NOT a 'residential sale' under the brokerage relationship disclosure rules?
c: A vacant lot intended for a duplex
ex: A residential sale is improved residential property of 4 units or fewer, unimproved residential property intended for 4 units or fewer, or agricultural property of 10 acres or fewer.

0: A single-family home is covered. The question asks which is NOT.
1: Land for 4 units or fewer is covered. The question asks which is NOT.
3: Agricultural property of 10 acres or fewer is covered. The question asks which is NOT.

q: A licensee rents an apartment to a tenant under a one-year lease with no option to buy. The brokerage relationship disclosure requirements:
c: apply, because the property is residential
apply only if the rent exceeds $1,000 a month
apply only if the tenant asks for a notice
ex: The disclosure requirements do not apply to leases, unless the lease includes an option to purchase property of 4 or fewer residential units.

0: A lease without a purchase option is outside the rule.
2: The rent amount is not the test.
3: A request does not bring a plain lease within the rule.

q: The Consent to Transition to Transaction Broker must be signed by:
c: the buyer customer of the brokerage
the principal of the single agent
ex: A single agent may change to a transaction broker only with the principal's written consent, given before the change.

0: The consent comes from the principal, who gives up single-agent duties.
3: The FREC does not sign consents.

q: A licensee sells a house at a real estate auction. The brokerage relationship disclosure requirements:
c: apply only to the winning bidder
apply only if the house sells above the reserve
ex: Auctions are among the situations where the disclosure requirements do not apply, along with appraisals, business sales and nonresidential transactions.

2: Auctions are an exception for everyone.

q: In which transaction may a broker appoint designated sales associates?
c: A $2 million house sale where both parties consent in writing
An office building sale where each party has assets of $1 million or more
Any sale of any property with a price above $1 million
A condominium sale in which the broker owns an interest
ex: Designated sales associates are allowed only when the transaction is not a residential sale and the buyer and the seller each have assets of $1 million or more, at their request and with signed disclosures.

2: The test is each party's assets, not the price.
3: The broker's interest is not the test.

q: Each designated sales associate owes the party he or she represents the duties of a:
ex: Each designated sales associate acts as a single agent for his or her party and gives the single-agent disclosures.

q: Which duties continue after a brokerage relationship ends?
ex: Confidentiality and accounting survive the end of the relationship.

0: Loyalty and obedience end with the relationship.
2: That duty ends with the relationship.
3: That duty ends with the relationship.

q: A buyer asks a licensee directly whether anyone has died in the house. The licensee knows of a suicide there. The licensee:
c: must say that no one has died there
may deny it, because the statute says it is not material
has no duty to volunteer it, but may not give a false answer
must disclose it in writing before any showing
ex: The statute removes the duty to disclose a death, homicide or suicide on the property. It does not remove the duty of honesty, so the licensee may not lie.

0: A false answer breaks the duty of honesty.
1: The statute does not permit a false answer.
3: A death on the property is not a fact that must be disclosed.

q: Which event ends a brokerage relationship?
c: A reduction of the listing price
ex: A brokerage relationship ends by performance, expiration, mutual agreement, revocation or renunciation, death or incapacity, destruction of the property, or the bankruptcy of the principal.

1: A price change does not end the relationship.
2: The relationship is with the brokerage and continues.
3: Negotiation does not end the relationship.

q: The government takes private land for a public highway and pays the owner just compensation. This is:
ex: Eminent domain is the taking of private property for public use with just compensation. The payment does not make it voluntary.

0: Escheat applies when an owner dies with no will and no heirs.
2: Adverse possession is a private person gaining title by possession.
3: Foreclosure follows a default on a debt.

q: Which of the following is a voluntary transfer of title?
c: A gift of land by deed
ex: Voluntary transfers are by deed (sale or gift) and by will. Descent, escheat, eminent domain, foreclosure and adverse possession are involuntary.

q: A person who dies without a valid will dies:
ex: Testate means with a will. Intestate means without one, and the property passes to the heirs by descent.

2: A devise is a gift of real property by will.
3: Escheat is the passing of property to the state when there are no heirs.

q: An owner dies without a will, leaving two children. Her real property passes to them by:
ex: Without a will, property passes to the heirs by descent. With a will, real property passes by devise.

2: Escheat applies only when there are no heirs.
3: Eminent domain is a government taking.

q: A man has openly lived on a rural lot for 8 years with the owner's permission. Can he claim title by adverse possession?
c: Yes, if he paid the taxes in the last year
No, because possession with permission is not hostile
No, because adverse possession takes 20 years
ex: Adverse possession requires possession that is open, notorious, hostile and continuous for 7 years, plus color of title or payment of taxes. Permission means the possession is not hostile.

0: Seven years alone is not enough. The possession must be hostile.
1: Taxes do not cure permissive possession.
3: Twenty years is the prescriptive easement period.

q: A will takes effect:
c: when it is signed before witnesses
when it is recorded in the county
at the death of the person who made it
ex: A will operates only at death and can be revoked until then.

1: Recording is not what gives a will effect.

q: In which deed does the grantor warrant the title only against defects that arose during the grantor's own ownership?
ex: A special warranty deed covers only defects arising during the grantor's ownership. A general warranty deed covers the whole history of the title.

0: A general warranty deed covers defects from any time.
2: A bargain and sale deed gives no warranties.

q: Which deed implies that the grantor owns the property but contains no warranties?
ex: A bargain and sale deed implies ownership but gives no warranties. A quitclaim deed does not even imply ownership.

0: A general warranty deed gives full warranties.
1: A special warranty deed warrants the grantor's period of ownership.
3: A quitclaim deed conveys only whatever interest the grantor has, if any.

q: Which deed gives the grantee the least protection?
